'outro' = perturbação textual controlada do prompt; 'instrucao' = descrição da tarefa em linguagem natural e prefixos/sufixos que reforçam que se trata de tarefa de código, mantidos inalterados. Contrafactual: a taxa 0,0 (prompt não perturbado) contra taxas de 0,1 a 1,0, com mesmos modelos, tarefas, prefixos/sufixos, temperatura e repetições. O efeito medido é a variação estrutural do código (similaridade TSED com as saídas do prompt original), não qualidade ou correção.

citacoes.trecho: To this end we propose an evaluation pipeline for LLM code generation with a focus on measuring sensitivity to prompt augmentations, completely agnostic to a specific programming tasks and LLMs, and thus widely applicable.
We apply three augmentation methods to the prompts: keyboard typos, synonyms, and paraphrasing.
This method attempts to simulate typos that a human can make while typing text on a keyboard.
Paraphrasing uses the translation capabilities of LLMs (i.e., Gemini) to paraphrase the prompt.
These reference outputs serve as ground truth representations of the model’s behavior on the original task specification.
To ensure all requests produce valid code, we added prefixes and postfixes, unaltered and ignored in the analysis, that stressed to the LLM that each request represents a coding task.
To reduce stochasticity of the results, we repeated each request to a LLM 5 times and recorded all responses, and we have also set the temperature of all models to 0.
Importantly, we do not evaluate correctness of generated code, and specifically focus on deviations between the codes generated from the original and altered prompts.
While temperature is considered to be the main parameter that gauges how random the output of a LLM is, even setting temperature to 0 does not guarantee fully deterministic results.
Llama 3.3 and Claude 3 Haiku, on the other hand, exhibit higher instability for unaltered prompts, again with temperature set to 0.
Unfortunately the most commonly circulated LeetCode tasks are included in the training data of most modern LLMs, which means they achieve almost 100% correct performance on these problems.
Matching their publication dates and official training cut-off dates of the LLMs we used, we have high confidence these tasks were not used in the training data for LLM models we evaluated.

Not only do we observe high variance for even unaltered prompts (only 0.7 similarity between generated code outputs), we can also confirm that code similarity drops below 0.5 TSED after only 10% of the prompt is modified, suggesting high sensitivity to these modifications.

Even on its own structural variability matters: users providing similar prompts may receive dramatically different implementations, affecting code review, maintenance, and trust, even when the code is functionally equivalent.
As mentioned before, TSED measures structural similarity, not functional equivalence, creating potential construct validity issues.
Structural variability poses real challenges for users who must understand, debug, and maintain different implementations.
We have also used multiple LLM providers in all our experiments to show how our method can be applied to different models.

The setup of the experiment was to instruct the LLM to adopt each persona in turn and to paraphrase a provided prompt, using their background and assumed knowledge to inform the language they use to describe the task and to add any details that they consider relevant.
We then randomly sampled one of these prompts for each persona and input it into the user interface of ChatGPT and Claude to generate the code.
The code generated by each persona on the three tasks and two models (ChatGPT and Claude) was evaluated observationally for trends.
We used all male personas in order to isolate whether programming experience influences prompt development and the resulting code without influence from gender bias in the training set of the LLM.

Using the framework from El-Assady et al. [9], we can see from the visualisation in Figure 4 the relative number of entities that are common between the prompts generated by the different personas by the thickness of the lines connecting the persona names in the visualisation.

This resulted in large differences in the generated code, with the most dramatic being no code generated when it asked for “the computer to write up a set of financial reports” for the accounting report generation task, which provided a set of instructions for how the user could send the reports in and it would then process them without providing a code implementation.

Specifically, the mean BERT score was 98.0%, with all 26532 recorded evaluations scoring above 91.0%, suggesting potential range restriction and ceiling effects that could negatively impact our experiments were they to use this metric [28].
A lower Sacre BLEU metric value indicates higher diversity.

The test revealed a statistically significant effect of augmentation rate on code similarity (p < 0.001 for keyboard typos and synonyms, p < 0.02 for paraphrasings), indicating a strong relationship between augmentation rate and LLM code generation sensitivity.

The test showed significant (p < 0.001 for keyboard typos and p < 0.02 for synonyms) difference in the distribution of sensitivity increases across three datasets, supporting the generalizability of our pipeline for a variety of programming tasks.
